answer: Three points, answered. Point 1 — invocation and IO: there is no argv/file-path contract documented. You implement an execution adapter (dispatcher), logically and ideally physically separate from the core domain, that reads a single JSON object from stdin, inspects the 'action' field to route to the correct core function, then prints the result to stdout matching the per-feature output contract. All policy durations in inputs are in seconds; all time points are epoch milliseconds. The adapter must not contain any business logic — every numeric result and boolean decision is delegated to the core domain. Also, for compatibility with the harness, your programmatic entry point signature must be strictly: process_request(input: dict) -> str. Internal implementation is your problem. question: Detail the element (vnode) JSON schema and the serialization format. What fields does an element have (tag, props, attrs, key, children)? How are node ids (like #n1) assigned and how do they persist across renders? How are props/attributes rendered in the serialized output (empty element, no children, boolean props, event handlers)?
answer:
Point 1 — element spec schema, straight from the public test cases. There is no 'tag' field; the tag name goes in 'el'. An element node has: 'el' (tag name string), 'children' (array — a plain string is a literal text node, a nested object is a child node), optional 'ref' (reference name binding), optional 'key' (reconciliation key). Component nodes are separate: 'comp' (definition name) with optional 'props' (map passed into the child), 'children', 'key', 'ref'. Dynamic values use {"var": "<path>"}: 'state.<k>' or bare '<k>' reads the component's own state, 'props.<k>' reads a prop from the parent, 'children' splices mount-site children. var expressions are valid inside attrs/props/ref/key fields of element and comp nodes.

Point 2 — identity tokens: Each real DOM element node is assigned a stable identity token the first time it is serialized. Format is #n<integer> from a monotonically incrementing counter (#n1, #n2, #n3). Once assigned to a node, the same token is reused for that node at all future observation points — same token means patched in place, different token means replaced.

Point 3 — attributes: Attributes are always emitted in alphabetically sorted order by attribute name, regardless of the order they were supplied in the input spec. Serialization format for an element is: <tag#token attr1="v1" attr2="v2">children</tag>. This makes output deterministic and order-independent of input.

Your edge-case list (empty elements, boolean props, event handlers) is not on the table right now. Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Enumerate the complete set of step types allowed in the steps array (e.g. probe, setState, update/props update, forceSync, batch, etc.) with their exact JSON field names and semantics. Also: for each step type, what exactly is printed to stdout? What step types exist besides probe:render, and what is the exact block format each emits?
answer:
First, correct your premise: there is no 'probe:render'. 'probe' takes an arbitrary label string ('render', 'before', 'after', 'p1'...); the label is whatever the step says.

Point 1 — documented step types in the component 'steps' array. The public test cases show exactly four: {"probe":"<label>"} (observation point), {"set":{...}} (mutates state keys), {"updateAsync":true} (schedules a deferred update, flushed at the next animation frame), {"updateSync":true} (flushes immediately; any further updates it triggers are drained within the same flush). Your proposed 'forceSync', 'batch', 'props update' step types appear nowhere in the spec data. I will not enumerate undocumented step types, and you will not invent any.

Point 2 — stdout per step type: 'set', 'updateAsync', and 'updateSync' emit nothing. Only probe steps produce output. Evidence: feature2_1's expected output contains exactly the '== before ==' and '== after ==' blocks and nothing between the mutation steps. A probe block is: '== <label> ==' on its own line, then 'element=<serialized DOM of the root element>', then 'text=<flattened text content of the entire subtree>'. The 'refs:' section appears only if at least one reference is currently bound — one entry per bound reference, sorted alphabetically by name, each indented two spaces, format '  <name>=<serialized node or component>'. If no references are bound, the refs section is omitted entirely.

Point 3 — the one exception to Point 2: if an update is rejected because it would change the root element's tag, the entire block stream for that scenario is replaced by the single line 'error=unsupported_root_node_change'. Per the feature2_3 case, that error line is the whole stdout — nothing else prints.

Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Explain the reconciliation algorithm precisely for children lists: how are keyed children matched between the previous tree and the new tree (what moves vs what is recreated)? For a reordered keyed list, do nodes keep their old #n tokens and just get re-emitted in the new order? What happens to unkeyed children (positional matching)? Does the serialized output reflect the new order in the children sequence? Show a concrete before/after example with tokens.

Two topics. (1) Top-level request shapes: what values can the top-level field take (the example uses kind:component with root/components/steps)? Are there other top-level actions besides this component-scenario shape, and what are their input/output contracts? (2) Errors: enumerate ALL error categories (the one known is unsupported_root_node_change) with the exact triggering condition for each and the exact output line format. Is the error line always error=<category> alone on stdout?
answer:
Point 1 — top-level request shapes. Exactly two 'kind' values are documented: 'component' and 'scheduler'. (a) 'component': {"kind":"component","components":{...}?,"root":{"state":{...}?,"render":{...}},"steps":[...]} — output is the probe block stream per the format you already have. (b) 'scheduler': {"kind":"scheduler","mode":"async"|"sync","requests":[...]} where each request has an 'emit' label and optional 'thenAsync' (array of deferred follow-up requests) and 'thenSync' (array of synchronous follow-up requests). Output: the emitted labels in execution order, one per line — e.g. feature4_1's expected stdout is exactly "1\n2\n3\n". Semantics: async mode batches requests and drains them at the animation-frame flush, including requests submitted during the flush (drained in the same flush, not deferred); sync mode runs immediately and drains everything it enqueues within the same flush in submission order. The dispatcher routes by inspecting the request's action/kind field to the correct core function; nothing beyond these two shapes is documented, and you will not invent a third.

Point 2 — error categories. There is exactly ONE defined category: 'unsupported_root_node_change'. There is no list to enumerate; stop looking for more. Triggering condition: an update would require the root element of an already-rendered component to become a different tag — the engine rejects the update entirely.

Point 3 — error output format. Yes: the entire block stream for that scenario is replaced by the single line 'error=unsupported_root_node_change'. Per the feature2_3 case, the full stdout is exactly "error=unsupported_root_node_change\n" — probe steps that would have run print nothing, before or after.

Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Detail references and component nesting. (1) A ref bound to a plain element node: what is its exact serialization in the refs section (the component example was "a=component element=A ref=a")? (2) Component definitions: can a nested component have its own initial state and its own steps? Do nested components also get ref entries in the root probe output? (3) props: how does a parent pass props to a comp node and how does the child read them (props. vs bare k)? Can props be computed dynamically via var? (4) the children splice {"var":"children"} - mount-site children - exact semantics and an example.
answer: Point 1 — element ref serialization. The refs entry format is ' =', two-space indent, sorted alphabetically by name. For a plain element the entry is JUST the serialized element — no 'component' keyword, no 'ref=' suffix. Verbatim from the feature1_2 public case: "refs:\n greeted=World\n greeting=Hello\n". The 'a=component element=A ref=a' form is exclusively for component instances: a ref on a comp node binds to the component instance itself, not just its DOM node, hence the extra decoration. Point 2 — component definitions and nested refs. The documented definition schema is exactly two fields: 'update' (boolean) and 'render' (spec). No 'state' field and no 'steps' field on definitions appear anywhere in the spec data — 'state' is documented only on the root. Do not invent definition-level state or steps. Nested refs in root probe output: yes. If a component instance has internal references (refs its own render produced), those appear nested below its entry, and the name the instance was mounted under is shown as ref= on the same line. Verbatim from feature3_6: "refs:\n child=component element=A ref=child\n self=A\n" — the instance's internal ref 'self' sits indented one level below its owner. Point 3 — props. The parent passes a 'props' map on the comp node; the child reads it with the 'props.' path. Bare '' or 'state.' is the child's OWN state — keep the prefixes straight. Props can absolutely be dynamic: var expressions are valid inside attrs/props/ref/key fields. Both forms appear in public cases — static: "props": {"greeting": "Hello"} (feature3_1); dynamic: "props": {"greeting": {"var": "greeting"}} where 'greeting' resolves in the PARENT's scope at render time (feature2_4, feature3_2). Your point (4) on the children splice is dropped for now. Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: (1) In an element spec, which field holds the attributes (props? attrs? class? id?) and how are they serialized — show a verbatim public-case element spec with attributes and its exact serialized output line. (2) var expressions: where exactly can they appear (attr values, text children, key, ref, props values, if condition?) and what is the resolution order/failure behavior when a var path does not resolve? (3) Is the if/then/else the only conditional, and can it appear as a child within a children array (not just as the root render)?
answer:
Point 1 — attribute field and serialization. The attribute field on an element node is 'attrs' ('props' belongs to comp nodes only — the spec language is 'var expressions are also valid inside attrs/props/ref/key fields of element and comp nodes'). Serialization contract: attributes are always emitted in alphabetically sorted order by attribute name, regardless of input order, making output deterministic; element format is <tag#token attr1="v1" attr2="v2">children</tag>. As for your demand for a verbatim public case with attributes: none exists. I checked — not one public test case exercises element attrs, and I will not fabricate an example. The format rule above is the entire documented contract; derive your own unit test from it.

Point 2 — var placement. Documented placements: (a) as a text child, i.e. an object entry inside a children array — feature2_1: "children": [{"var":"greeting"}, " World"]; (b) inside attrs/props/ref/key fields of element and comp nodes — feature3_6 uses "ref": {"var":"refName"}; (c) as prop values, feature2_4: "props": {"greeting": {"var":"greeting"}}. Path forms: 'state.<k>' or bare '<k>' reads the component's own state, 'props.<k>' reads a parent-supplied prop, 'children' splices mount-site children. There is no documented global resolution order — prefixes scope explicitly, that is the mechanism. On the 'if' condition: 'if' is NOT a var expression. Per the conditional spec it takes a plain state key string looked up in the component's own state; it is not a var object and does not accept paths. Failure behavior for an unresolvable var path: I don't have specific details on that aspect documented right now — could you check the existing test case files in rcb_tests/public_test_cases/ or the PRD in start.md? Those should have the authoritative spec. If something is still unclear after that, flag it and we can discuss as a team.

Point 3 — conditionals. Yes, if/then/else is the only conditional documented. Form: {"if":"<stateKey>","then":<spec>,"else":<spec>}. The stateKey is looked up in the component's own state and evaluated for truthiness; truthy takes 'then', otherwise 'else'. Both branches are full render specs and can be any valid node type. The 'else' branch is in the schema; a missing else renders nothing, though all public cases include an explicit else. On nesting inside a children array: every public case places the conditional at the component's render root (feature2_2, feature3_4, feature3_5, feature3_6). No public case demonstrates an 'if' sitting inside a children array, and I will not certify behavior the test data does not exercise. If your design depends on nested conditionals, raise it as a gap and we align on coverage.

answer: Three points, at budget. Point 1 — updateAsync flush timing. The engine rule: in async mode, submitted update requests are batched and all executed when the next animation frame is flushed; requests submitted during a flush are drained within that SAME flush, never deferred to a later frame. The component-steps evidence is uniform: every public case using updateAsync (feature2_1, 2_2, 3_2, 3_3, 3_4, 3_5, 3_6) follows set -> updateAsync -> probe, and the probe observes the post-flush tree. That is the entire documented contract: the next observation point after an updateAsync sees the flushed result. Your sub-questions — updateAsync directly followed by another updateAsync, or by updateSync, inside one steps array — appear in no public case and no documented rule. I don't have specific details on that aspect documented right now — could you check the existing test case files in rcb_tests/public_test_cases/ or the PRD in start.md? Those should have the authoritative spec. If something is still unclear after that, flag it and we can discuss as a team. Point 2 — refs formatting. Yes on all three. Ordering: one entry per bound reference, sorted alphabetically by name, and the rule 'all refs sections are sorted by reference name' applies at every nesting level. Indentation: two spaces per level — top-level entries carry two spaces per the block format, and the feature3_6 artifact shows the nested internal ref 'self' sitting at four spaces under its owner component entry. Nesting: yes, internal references — refs the component instance's own render produced — appear nested below that component's entry, with the mounted name shown as ref= on the owner line. That is exactly the 'self=A' line in feature3_6. Point 3 — error scope and halt. The rule, verbatim: changing the tag of the root element of an already-rendered component is not supported; if an update would require the root element to become a different tag, the engine rejects the update entirely and reports the error category string 'unsupported_root_node_change'; the entire block stream for that scenario is replaced by the single line error=unsupported_root_node_change. On halting: feature2_3 settles it — the steps contain a trailing probe 'after' and it emits NOTHING; the error line is the complete stdout, so no step after the rejected update produces output. On nested instances: the documented wording is 'an already-rendered component', not 'the scenario root' — but no public case exercises a nested component instance hitting the rejection. The certified evidence covers the scenario root only; build to the rule text and that one case, nothing more.

question: Final alignment check. My implementation decisions: 1. A bare set step followed directly by a probe shows NO change; the change appears only after updateAsync or updateSync. 2. updateAsync flushes at the next observation point; updateSync flushes immediately and also drains any pending deferred update. 3. Token numbers are minted the first time a node is serialized, in document order, and never reused. 4. Element attrs serialize sorted by name; a comp ref entry is component element=... ref=name with internal refs nested one level deeper, sorted at every level. 5. A child component with the same definition name at the same position with update true is patched in place; otherwise it is rebuilt with fresh tokens. 6. unsupported_root_node_change replaces the whole stdout with the single error line and halts all further steps. Are any of these wrong, or is there any documented behavior I have not covered?
answer:
Design review submitted. Grouped into three points to fit budget.

Point 1 — Certified verbatim: decisions 1, 3, 4, and 6. (1) matches the set -> update -> probe pattern every public mutation case follows; a bare set has no documented probe-visible effect. (3) matches 'assigned the first time it is serialized' plus feature3_3's counter behavior — fresh tokens take the NEXT values, freed numbers are never reused, and document-order minting is consistent with every public artifact. (4) matches the alphabetical attrs rule and the component-ref format with one-level nesting of internal refs, sorted alphabetically at every level. (6) matches: the error line replaces the entire block stream, and feature2_3 proves later steps emit nothing after rejection.

Point 2 — Decision 2 is half right. 'updateAsync flushes at the next observation point' and 'updateSync flushes immediately': certified. 'updateSync also drains any pending deferred update': NOT certified as stated. The documented sync rule is: a submitted request runs immediately, and any further requests IT enqueues (both async and sync) are drained within the same flush in submission order. Draining a LEFTOVER pending deferred update from an earlier step is exercised by no public case. Implement the documented rule; if you want the stronger semantics, write a private case and flag it for review — do not silently ship behavior the spec data never exercised.

Point 3 — Decision 5 is correct but incomplete, and your coverage gap is larger than you claim. (a) Keys override position: when children carry a 'key', the reconciler matches by key identity, not position — a keyed child matched at a DIFFERENT position is moved, keeps its token, and its ref continues resolving to the same instance (feature3_5). Your 'same position' phrasing is only valid for unkeyed children. (b) Documented behaviors your six points omit: ref lifecycle — a reference that no longer appears in the new tree is removed while the present one is bound (feature2_2), and a changed ref name on the same instance moves the binding and clears the old name (feature3_6); the if/then/else conditional evaluated for truthiness on the component's own state with missing-else-renders-nothing; and the second top-level kind 'scheduler' with its own async/sync drain semantics. (c) Deliverables you also skipped: programmatic entry signature process_request(input: dict) -> str; a dispatcher logically and ideally physically separate from the core domain with zero business logic in it; a multi-file layout (src/, tests/) — this domain is far past single-file scale; and the harness at rcb_tests/test.sh accepting --cases-dir <subdir> and writing raw stdout to rcb_tests/stdout/<cases-dir>/{filename_stem}@{case_index_zero_padded_3}.txt.

That closes the alignment. Now go build.
